rating.reasoning_summary: This strand centers on Patrick McKenzie's (patio11) concept of 'The Sort'—a societal mechanism that increasingly efficiently allocates talent to high-leverage positions based on IQ and other markers. The boundary object is his viral August 2024 thread anthropomorphizing this emergent system. The discourse is primarily constructive rather than dialectical: people recognize, apply, and extend the concept to explain endogamy, educational decline, ethnic formation, and career paths. Evolution is medium: the idea spreads and gets applied to new domains (ethnicity, humanities, Cocomelon kids) but doesn't fundamentally transform. The strand lacks deep counter-arguments or refinement through conflict—it's more memetic adoption than knowledge production.

title: “The Sort” is coming for your life path
summary:
Patrick McKenzie (@patio11) dropped a perfectly ominous line — “The good news: we got much better at running The Sort. The bad news: we got much better at running The Sort.” — and suddenly everyone had a name for the creepy thing they’ve felt for years: society as a talent dragnet that hunts for high-leverage people, yanks them out of whatever random hometown trajectory they were on, and funnels them into a narrow set of elite tracks. His best bit is the cold, inhuman vibe: The Sort doesn’t “feel” anything, but it does look at your life and call it “inefficient.” He even uses his own family as the gut-punch example: his dad “should” have been swapped with the worst lawyer, and Patrick himself “squandered a decade” before landing where The Sort would’ve put him earlier.

The thread caught because it’s not just “IQ matters” — it’s “the system is self-aware and lies.” McKenzie claims The Sort knows people hate hearing how it works, so it “fibs about them as a stakeholder management strategy,” and even your ability to decode the fibs is itself something The Sort selects for. Replies mostly nodded along and extended the metaphor: Tim Galebach (@TimGalebach) framed it as rising leverage in knowledge work (sorted people end up where the multipliers are); @alexpotato talked about having to route around The Sort without Ivy/math credentials to reach “hedge fund land.” A few tried to poke holes — @verbine called the underlying IQ/income graph a “methodological mess” that misses the 130+ tail The Sort would actually care about; @tesavova wondered if the correlation is lower than advertised because incomes got more extreme (fatter top-end tail, not necessarily better sorting).

Then the meme escaped containment. People started using “The Sort” as a universal solvent for other anxieties: Bryan Caplan (@bryan_caplan) claimed humanities prof IQs have crashed since the 80s and someone immediately replied “the sort will continue until morale improves”; @eigenrobot connected it to ethnogenesis via endogamy (if groups self-select and marry within the sorted strata long enough, you get new “ethnic” formations); and the discourse hit full brain-poison with the viral “non-Cocomelon kids will financially enslave the others” quote getting folded in as a Sort-shaped generational prophecy. The peak wasn’t a big refutation — it was adoption: “Sort” became the shorthand for why careers, cities, mating, academia, even kid media feel like they’re getting algorithmically stratified. You’d care because once you see it, you start asking the uncomfortable follow-up that @__venki__ and @tr_babb voiced later: should we weaken The Sort — and if we could, would that be merciful… or just mean?
